title: Hop to the Last Square
statement:
A row of squares is numbered from 0. You start on square 0. Standing on square i, you may hop forward by any whole number of squares from 1 up to hops[i]. A square with hops[i] = 0 is a dead end.

Return true if some sequence of hops lands you on the last square, and false otherwise. Hopping past the end is not possible, but a hop that could reach further than the last square may simply be shortened.

examples.why: Hop 1 to square 1, then hop 3 to square 4. Always taking the longest hop lands on square 2, a dead end, and wrongly gives false.
From squares 0 and 1 you can reach at most square 3, and squares 2 and 3 are both dead ends. The 4 on the last square never matters.
0 → 2 → 4. You hop over both inner zeros, so "any zero means false" is wrong. A zero on the last square is fine: you are already there.

hints: You do not need to know which path gets you somewhere, only whether you can get there.
If you can reach square j, can you also reach every square before j? Think about the hop that got you past them.
Keep one number: the farthest square reachable so far. Walk forward; if you ever stand beyond it, you are stuck.

explain.intuition:
The reachable squares always form a solid block starting at 0. Why: if you can reach square j, the hop that took you there started at some k < j and could have been shortened to stop at any square between k and j. So there are no holes, and one number describes everything you know: far, the end of the block.

Now walk the squares in order. Each square i inside the block can stretch it to i + hops[i]. Taking the max never hurts, because a bigger block contains every square a smaller one does. If you ever step onto a square i > far, nothing behind you reaches it and nothing ahead of you is reachable either, so the answer is false. Note what the greedy does not do: it never commits to a hop. "Always hop as far as possible" is a different rule, and example 1 breaks it.
steps: For each square i from left to right: if i > far, return false.
As soon as far ≥ n − 1, return true. (Or return true after the loop.)
pitfalls: Simulating one path by always taking the longest hop. Example 1 lands on a dead end that a shorter hop avoids.
Returning false whenever you meet a zero. A zero only matters if far cannot get past it, as in [2, 0, 2, 0, 0].
Checking the dead end on the last square. Once you stand on it you are done, whatever its value.

solutions.title: Mark every reachable square
solutions.idea: Walk forward. From each square already marked reachable, mark every square its hop covers.

solutions.title: Move the goal backwards
solutions.idea: Walk from the right. A square is good if it can reach the current goal; when it can, it becomes the new goal. The answer is whether the goal ends at 0.

solutions.title: Track the farthest reachable square
solutions.idea: The reachable squares form a block from 0. Grow its end with every square inside it; fail if you step outside.

followups: Return the fewest hops needed instead of yes or no.
Hops may now go backwards as well as forwards. Why does the greedy break, and what replaces it?
